kicker: The fish reads no books about water — it swims. Robots too: they have to practise; reading alone is not enough.
summary: Robots now run faster than people — but finding their own way and holding a cup of tea are still hard.

quiz.q: A robot understands “pick up the teacup” at once, but its hand still slips. Why?
options: There is little real grasping data for robots to learn from
The motors in the robot's hand are still far too weak to grip
The command was not written clearly enough
The teacup is too heavy for the robot's hand
quiz.explain: The head learns from the mountain of text online. The hand has to learn from real grasps — and that kind of data is very scarce.

race.label: The finish line draws nearer
race.art: A low camera runs behind an ink robot on a track that curves round a moonlit lake; pines and stone lanterns slide past on the right, a bamboo rail keeps the human lane apart. Drag the moon through the racing seasons: in 2025 the robot staggers and falls, another lies on the track; in March 2026 a mist-white runner sets the record in the next lane; in April 2026 the robot strides past it and the red ribbon breaks across its chest, leaving two finish lines on the track at two depths. Today the camera cranes up and the valley behind the lake is dotted with factory lamps.
race.prompt: Drag the moon left through the racing seasons
race.moonAria: Drag the moon, or use the ← → keys to move through the milestones

fact.text: At the first robot half marathon, the winning robot (Tiangong Ultra) took 2 hours 40 minutes 42 seconds; many robots fell or dropped out.
Runner Jacob Kiplimo (Uganda) set the men's half marathon record: 57 minutes 20 seconds, in Lisbon.
Honor's self-navigating robot “Lightning” (Shandian) won the 21 km in 50 minutes 26 seconds — almost 7 minutes faster than the human record.

horizon.text: Running fast has arrived; doing housework on its own is still an open question — and predictions of when differ wildly.

insight.text: In just one year, the robot finished three times faster: from 2 hours 41 minutes to 50 minutes — faster than the human record.

detail.text: Robots and people ran in separate lanes: this compares times; it was not one shared race.

strings.label: Walking alone or on strings
strings.art: Low at the finish line: two identical ink robots run toward us with the moon behind them. On a pine bough a person in a conical hat holds a control bar and a small lamp. The robot on the right lights its own way with its lamp eyes; the one on the left has dark eyes. Pull the bar: threads tighten from it to the left robot's head, hands and knee and catch the moonlight. Drag sideways to walk round: head-on the threads almost vanish, from the side they shine.
strings.prompt: Touch the robot on the left: who is steering it?
steps: Drag sideways to see the strings from the side

strings.turnAria: Walk round the finish line: drag sideways or use ← →

facts.text: Race rule: a robot steered by a person has its time multiplied by 1.2 — 48:19 becomes 57:59.

detail.text: Only just over 40% of teams let their robot find its own way; the rest steered remotely.

insight.text: “Can walk” is not “knows the way”: a robot steered by a person may be faster, but a person still watches the road.

teacup.label: A mountain of words, a basket of moves
teacup.art: A stone tea table under a paper lantern: a celadon cup, a clay teapot and a tiny bamboo basket with a few paper rolls of “hand data”. A many-jointed robot arm reaches in from the right; the robot's head is a lantern. Behind, blurred in mist, a mountain of book spines climbs into the clouds. Pull a bamboo slip: the head lights up at once, while the hand trembles, slips and tries again.

insight.text: The robot's head understands the command at once. The hand trembles and slips: it has not practised enough.

data.text: Moves for robots to learn from: the Open X-Embodiment collection holds over 1 million manipulations
Words for AI to learn from: Llama 3 read more than 15 trillion pieces of text (tokens)

insight2.text: The hard part is the “hands” more than the “head”: text online is as plentiful as mountains, but real grasping data is scarce.

teacup.common: Two different units — but one is a mountain, the other a basket.
teacup.detail: The faint cup you just saw was the robot's own guess: the cup will spill if tipped too far. AI that practises guessing like this is called a “world model”.

circle.label: Does it need a human shape?
circle.art: At the water's edge looking out over the moon lake: four equal boulders stand in the shallows, each crossed by a gold seam. Touch each one: it cracks along the seam, its halves open like a seed, and a small lamp inside lights a carving: a human shape, a factory arm, a broken stair going down, an empty chair in a doorway.

stones.who: Figure AI · a humanoid robot company (2022)

view.text: The world is built for humans, so general-purpose robots in human form are the path with the greatest impact.

stones.who: The specialised-robot camp · robot counts from the IFR (09/2026)

view.text: About 5 million robots work in factories (IFR figures) — not one of them has legs. This camp says: repetitive work needs specialised machines.

stones.who: Those worried about jobs · economists Acemoglu & Restrepo

view.text: A US study (1990–2007, factory robots): one more robot per 1,000 workers meant roughly 2–3 more people out of work in every 1,000.

stones.who: Rodney Brooks · roboticist, co-founder of iRobot (09/2025)

view.text: Full-size humanoid robots are not yet safe to stand near; he advises keeping 3 metres away, and guesses it will be over 10 years before they turn a profit.

common.text: Running fast on a track is not working in a home. The question left: in what shape will robots enter our lives?

ap-robot-2026.title: A humanoid robot sprints past the human half-marathon world record in Beijing race
ap-robot-2026.note: The AP story recalls the 2025 race: the winning robot took 2:40:42 and many robots fell or did not finish. The page blocks lookup tools; content cross-checked via the KUOW and Interesting Engineering versions.

chinadaily-robot.title: Robots outrun humans at Beijing half marathon
chinadaily-robot.note: Honor's robot “Flash” won the self-navigating category in 50:26; over 40% of teams navigated autonomously; more than 100 teams (nearly 20 in 2025). Jacob Kiplimo's human record of 57:20 was set in Lisbon in March.

ie-robot.title: Humanoid robot surpasses human world record
ie-robot.note: A remote-controlled version of the same robot finished in 48:19; the winner is named “Lightning”. The robot's name varies between outlets (Lightning / Flash / Shandian 闪电).

beijing-gov-robot.title: Who is Winner? Champion Crowned for Humanoid Robot Half Marathon
beijing-gov-robot.note: Official information: the robot “Shandian” (闪电) of team Monkey King won in 50:26; remote-controlled robots' times were multiplied by 1.2.

aljazeera-robot.title: Humanoid robot breaks half marathon world record in Beijing
aljazeera-robot.note: People and robots ran in separate lanes to avoid collisions; according to CCTV, the winning robot averaged about 25 km/h.

ifr-2026.title: Five Million Robots Now Operate in Factories Globally
ifr-2026.note: World Robotics 2026 report (2025 data): 5 million industrial robots in operation, more than 600,000 newly installed that year.

gemini-robotics.title: Gemini Robotics brings AI into the physical world
gemini-robotics.note: A vision–language–action (VLA) model built on Gemini 2.0, adding physical movement as an output.

oxe-2023.title: Open X-Embodiment: Robotic Learning Datasets and RT-X Models
oxe-2023.note: Over 1 million recorded manipulations from 22 kinds of robot, contributed by 21 institutions.

meta-llama3.title: Introducing Meta Llama 3
meta-llama3.note: Llama 3 was pretrained on over 15 trillion tokens from publicly available sources.

figure-master-plan.title: Master Plan
figure-master-plan.note: The view of the humanoid robot company itself.

nber-robots.title: Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets
nber-robots.publisher: NBER Working Paper 23285 (Daron Acemoglu, Pascual Restrepo); final version in the Journal of Political Economy, 2020
nber-robots.note: A study of industrial robots in the US over 1990–2007, not humanoid robots.

brooks-2025.title: Why Today's Humanoids Won't Learn Dexterity
brooks-2025.note: Personal essay: without a sense of touch and force, robots struggle to become dexterous; advises not standing within 3 metres of a walking full-size robot.
